```{r knitr-opts, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```


**Base treatment (fixed across all interaction models in this series):**
`W = 1(type == 1)` vs. `type == 0`, restricted to
`name_ethnicity %in% c("Canada", "Chinese", "Indian", "Pakistani")`. Type 0 to
Type 1 changes *only* the applicant's name --- education and work-experience
origin are held at "Canadian" for both --- so `W` isolates the pure name
effect, uncontaminated by the foreign-credential confounds present in Types
2--4. This is narrower than the Type 0--4 comparison used in the Table 4/5
baseline replication, and matches TC's instruction to restrict the causal
forest step to this cleaner contrast.

**This model's moderator:** `extracurricular_skills`, i.e. whether the resume lists
additional extracurricular activities. This directly operationalizes the statistical
discrimination test in Oreopoulos (2011) and Phelps (1972): the name penalty
should shrink when a resume supplies a stronger, unambiguous productivity
signal.

**On standard errors.** The original Stata code uses `robust` SEs only,
never clustering. Our own group proposal specifies clustering by `firmid`
instead, since ~4 resumes are sent to each employer in most waves. Both are
reported below side by side so the deviation is explicit and auditable rather
than silently substituted.

# Setup

```{r setup}
required_packages <- c("haven", "estimatr", "dplyr", "modelsummary")
missing_packages  <- setdiff(required_packages, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_packages, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}
library(haven)
library(estimatr)
library(dplyr)
library(modelsummary)

data_path <- file.path("data", "oreopoulos-resume-study-replication-data-file.dta")
if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  stop("Data file not found. Expected it at: ", normalizePath(data_path, mustWork = FALSE))
}
df <- read_dta(data_path)
```

# Sample construction

```{r sample}
df_int1 <- df %>%
  filter(
    type %in% c(0, 1),
    name_ethnicity %in% c("Canada", "Chinese", "Indian", "Pakistani")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    W              = as.numeric(type == 1),   # 1 = foreign name (Type 1), 0 = Type 0 baseline
    fall_data      = factor(fall_data),
    female                 = ifelse(is.na(female), 0, female),
    ba_quality              = ifelse(is.na(ba_quality), 0, ba_quality),
    language_skills         = ifelse(is.na(language_skills), 0, language_skills),
    ma                      = ifelse(is.na(ma), 0, ma),
    same_exp                = ifelse(is.na(same_exp), 0, same_exp),
    exp_highquality         = ifelse(is.na(exp_highquality), 0, exp_highquality),
    extracurricular_skills  = ifelse(is.na(extracurricular_skills), 0, extracurricular_skills)
  )

cat("Analysis sample size:", nrow(df_int1), "\n")
cat("Treatment (W) distribution:\n")
print(table(df_int1$W))
```

# Model: `callback ~ W * extracurricular_skills + controls`

```{r fit}
# (1) Robust SEs only -- matching Oreopoulos's original approach
m_robust <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ W + extracurricular_skills + W:extracurricular_skills + female + ba_quality +
           language_skills + ma + same_exp + exp_highquality + fall_data,
  data = df_int1, se_type = "HC1"
)

# (2) Clustered by firmid
m_clustered <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ W + extracurricular_skills + W:extracurricular_skills + female + ba_quality +
             language_skills + ma + same_exp + exp_highquality + fall_data,
  data = df_int1, clusters = firmid, se_type = "CR2"
)
```

## Combined table

```{r table, results = "asis"}
modelsummary(
  list(
    "Robust SE (Oreopoulos-style)" = m_robust,
    "Clustered by firm (proposal)"  = m_clustered
  ),
  stars    = TRUE,
  coef_omit = "fall_data",
  gof_omit  = "IC|Log|Adj|F|RMSE",
  title     = "Interaction Model 1: Name Penalty x Extracurricular Signal (Type 0 vs. Type 1)"
)
```

The coefficient of interest is `W:extracurricular_skills`. A positive and significant estimate means that listing extracurricular activities reduces the name penalty associated with having a foreign name. Specifically, the positive interaction coefficient of 0.031 indicates that the difference in callback rates between foreign- and baseline-name applicants becomes 0.031 larger when extracurricular skills are listed. This is consistent with statistical discrimination, as employers appear to respond to an observable signal of applicant quality that reduces their reliance on the name as a signal of expected productivity.
